cmimc-2019-power-01a.title: Read the definition
cmimc-2019-power-01a.body: $0^n1^n$ is $n$ zeros followed by $n$ ones: $\varepsilon,\,01,\,0011,\,000111,\dots$ So $L$ is the language of all strings that begin with some number of $0$s and end with the same number of $1$s, with nothing in between.

cmimc-2019-power-01b.title: Read the definition
cmimc-2019-power-01b.body: A word of the form $ww^r$ reads the same forwards and backwards and has even length $2|w|$. Conversely, every even-length palindrome is of this form (take $w$ to be its first half). So $M$ is the set of even-length palindromes.

cmimc-2019-power-01c.title: Both inclusions
cmimc-2019-power-01c.body:
**Every string in $O$ is balanced.** By induction on the construction: $\varepsilon$ is balanced, and $1u0v$, $0u1v$ add one $0$ and one $1$ to the balanced strings $u,v$.

**Every balanced string is in $O$.** Induct on the length. Let $w$ be balanced and non-empty, say $w$ starts with $1$ (the other case is symmetric). Score $+1$ for each $1$ and $-1$ for each $0$; the partial sums start at $1$ and end at $0$, so there is a first position where the sum returns to $0$. Then $w=1u0v$, where $u$ has total score $0$ (it is balanced) and $v$ is balanced; both are shorter, hence in $O$, so $w\in O$.

So $O$ is exactly the set of strings with equally many $0$s and $1$s.

cmimc-2019-power-02.title: Ignore the witness
cmimc-2019-power-02.body:
Let $L\in\mathsf P$ and let $A$ be a polynomial-time algorithm deciding $L$. Define the verifier $V(w,k)$: run $A(w)$ and return its answer (ignoring $k$).

- If $w\in L$, then $A(w)$ accepts, so $V(w,k)$ accepts for every $k$; in particular a witness exists.
- If $w\notin L$, then $A(w)$ rejects, so $V(w,k)$ rejects for every $k$: no witness exists.

$V$ runs in polynomial time because $A$ does. Hence $L\in\mathsf{NP}$. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-03a.title: Membership and hardness
cmimc-2019-power-03a.body:
**In $\mathsf{NP}$:** a witness is a coloring; checking that it uses at most $k$ colors and that adjacent vertices differ takes polynomial time.

**$\mathsf{NP}$-hard:** an instance $G$ of 3COL is the instance $(G,3)$ of COL. So a polynomial-time algorithm for COL would solve 3COL, and hence (as 3COL is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard) all of $\mathsf{NP}$.

cmimc-2019-power-03b.title: Membership and reduction
cmimc-2019-power-03b.body:
**In $\mathsf{NP}$:** the witness is the sublist; its sum is computed in polynomial time.

**$\mathsf{NP}$-hard:** let $L$ be a PARTITION instance with total $x$. Double every entry to get $2L$, which has total $2x$; then $L$ has a partition into two equal-sum parts iff $2L$ has a sublist of sum $x$ (equivalently: $L$ has a sublist with sum $x/2$). Thus the SUBSET-SUM instance $(2L,x)$ answers PARTITION on $L$, so a fast SUBSET-SUM algorithm would solve PARTITION.

cmimc-2019-power-03c.title: Membership and reduction
cmimc-2019-power-03c.body:
**In $\mathsf{NP}$:** the witness is one of the two parts; its sum is checked in polynomial time.

**$\mathsf{NP}$-hard:** given a SUBSET-SUM instance $(L,t)$ with $x=\sum L$, form $L'=L\cup\{2t-x\}$ if $2t\ge x$, and $L'=L\cup\{x-2t\}$ if $2t<x$. We show $(L,t)$ is a yes-instance iff $L'$ can be partitioned.

*Case $2t\ge x$.* The total of $L'$ is $2t$, so each side must have sum $t$. ($\Rightarrow$) If $S\subseteq L$ has sum $t$, take $S$ and its complement together with the new element ($x-t+2t-x=t$). ($\Leftarrow$) One of the two sides does not contain the new element; it is a sublist of $L$ with sum $t$.

*Case $2t<x$.* The total of $L'$ is $2x-2t$, so each side must have sum $x-t$. ($\Rightarrow$) If $S\subseteq L$ has sum $t$, put $S$ with the new element ($t+x-2t=x-t$) on one side and $L\setminus S$ (sum $x-t$) on the other. ($\Leftarrow$) The side without the new element is a sublist of $L$ of sum $x-t$; its complement in $L$ has sum $t$.

The construction takes polynomial time, so a fast algorithm for PARTITION would solve SUBSET-SUM.

cmimc-2019-power-04a.title: Bipartite
cmimc-2019-power-04a.body:
The graph is the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$: the three vertices in the left column are each joined to all three in the right column and to none in their own column. Coloring the left column red and the right column blue is proper, and one color is not enough because the graph has an edge. So $\chi=2$.

**Answer: 2**

cmimc-2019-power-04b.title: Odd cycle and explicit coloring
cmimc-2019-power-04b.body:
This is the Petersen graph. It contains the $5$-cycle formed by the outer pentagon, and an odd cycle needs $3$ colors, so $\chi\ge3$.

A $3$-coloring: label the outer vertices $o_0,\dots,o_4$ around the pentagon and let $i_k$ be the inner vertex joined to $o_k$; the inner vertices form a pentagram, with $i_k\sim i_{k\pm2}$. Color $o_0,\dots,o_4$ with $1,2,1,2,3$ and $i_0,\dots,i_4$ with $2,3,3,1,1$ respectively.

Check: each $i_k$ differs from its spoke partner $o_k$ ($2\ne1$, $3\ne2$, $3\ne1$, $1\ne2$, $1\ne3$); the outer cycle $1,2,1,2,3$ is proper (including $o_4o_0$: $3\ne1$); and the pentagram edges are proper: $i_0i_2$: $2,3$; $i_2i_4$: $3,1$; $i_4i_1$: $1,3$; $i_1i_3$: $3,1$; $i_3i_0$: $1,2$. So $\chi=3$.

**Answer: 3**

cmimc-2019-power-04c.title: The Moser spindle
cmimc-2019-power-04c.body:
Call the top vertex $T$, the two middle vertices $M_1$ (left) and $M_2$ (right), the side vertices $L,R$ and the bottom vertices $B_L,B_R$. The edges are $TL,TR,TM_1,TM_2,LM_2,RM_1,LB_L,RB_R,B_LB_R,B_LM_2,B_RM_1$.

**At least 4.** Triangles $TLM_2$ and $LM_2B_L$ share the edge $LM_2$. In a proper $3$-coloring the two triangles use all three colors, so $T$ and $B_L$ must receive the same color (the one not used on $L,M_2$). Likewise triangles $TRM_1$ and $RM_1B_R$ force $T$ and $B_R$ to have the same color. Then $B_L$ and $B_R$ have the same color, but they are adjacent: contradiction. So $\chi\ge4$.

**4 suffice.** $T=1$, $L=2$, $M_2=3$, $B_L=1$, $R=2$, $M_1=3$, $B_R=4$ is a proper coloring (check each of the $11$ edges).

**Answer: 4**

cmimc-2019-power-05.title: Greedy coloring
cmimc-2019-power-05.body: Order the vertices $v_1,\dots,v_n$ arbitrarily and color them in turn, giving $v_i$ the smallest color in $\{1,\dots,\Delta+1\}$ not already used on a neighbour of $v_i$. Such a color exists: $v_i$ has at most $\Delta$ neighbours, so at most $\Delta$ of the $\Delta+1$ colors are forbidden. The resulting coloring is proper, so $\chi(G)\le\Delta+1$. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-06.title: BFS 2-coloring
cmimc-2019-power-06.body:
Process each connected component separately. Pick a vertex, color it red, and run a breadth-first search, giving each newly reached vertex the color opposite to the vertex from which it was reached.

*Correctness.* If $G$ is $2$-colorable, then in any proper $2$-coloring the neighbours of a red vertex must all be blue and vice versa; so within a connected component the coloring is forced once the first vertex is colored, up to swapping the two colors. Our search produces exactly this forced coloring, so it is a proper coloring, using $1$ color for edgeless graphs and $2$ otherwise, which equals $\chi(G)$. The search takes $O(|V|+|E|)$ time. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-07a.title: Count the colors
cmimc-2019-power-07a.body:
Let $G$ be $3$-colorable on $n$ vertices (assume $\chi(G)=3$; for $\chi\le2$ the problem is easier).

*The loop.* The neighbourhood of any vertex is $2$-colorable (otherwise, together with $v$ it would need $4$ colors), so each iteration uses $1+2=3$ new colors. Each iteration deletes $v$ and at least $\sqrt n$ neighbours, so there are fewer than $\sqrt n$ iterations; the loop uses at most $3\sqrt n$ colors.

*The finish.* When the loop ends the remaining graph has maximum degree $<\sqrt n$, so by Problem 1.5 it needs at most $\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\approx\sqrt n$ further colors.

*Total:* at most $4\sqrt n$ colors (up to rounding $\sqrt n$ up), while $\mathrm{OPT}=\chi(G)=3$. So the algorithm is a $\frac{4\sqrt n}{3}=\frac43\sqrt n$-approximation. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-07b.title: Do not spend a color on $v$
cmimc-2019-power-07b.body:
Modify the loop body: pick $v$ of largest degree, **2-color the neighbourhood $N(v)$ with two fresh colors** (it is $2$-colorable since $G$ is $3$-colorable), and delete only $N(v)$ (not $v$). After the deletion $v$ is an isolated vertex of the remaining graph, so it will be colored later in the final stage at no extra cost.

*Number of iterations.* Each iteration deletes at least $\sqrt n$ vertices (the neighbours of a vertex of degree $\ge\sqrt n$), so there are at most $n/\sqrt n=\sqrt n$ iterations, using at most $2\sqrt n$ colors. (The loop terminates because $v$ keeps no neighbours.)

*Finish.* The remaining graph has maximum degree $<\sqrt n$, so Problem 1.5 colors it with at most $\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\approx\sqrt n$ colors (including $v$).

Total at most $3\sqrt n$ colors (up to rounding), i.e. a ratio of $3\sqrt n/3=\sqrt n$ against $\mathrm{OPT}=3$. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-08.title: Induction on $k$ (sketch with the main estimate)
cmimc-2019-power-08.body:
Let $a_k=1-\frac1{k-1}$, so the claim is: a $k$-colorable graph on $n$ vertices gets at most $\approx 2k\,n^{a_k}$ colors. The base case $k=2$ is exact (Problem 1.6: $2\le 4\lceil n^0\rceil$).

**Step $k\to k+1$.** Let the loop run $m$ times; the $i$-th time it recurses on a neighbourhood $H_i$ of size $h_i$ (which is $k$-colorable since $G$ is $(k+1)$-colorable). Each $h_i\ge n^{1-1/k}$ (the degree threshold), and $\sum h_i\le n$, so
$$m\le n^{1/k}.$$
By induction the recursive call uses at most $2k\,h_i^{a_k}$ colors (ignoring ceilings), plus $1$ color for $v$. The function $t\mapsto t^{a_k}$ is concave ($0<a_k<1$), so by Jensen
$$\sum_{i=1}^m h_i^{a_k}\le m\Bigl(\frac{\sum h_i}{m}\Bigr)^{a_k}\le m^{1-a_k}n^{a_k}\le n^{\frac1{k(k-1)}}\,n^{1-\frac1{k-1}}=n^{1-\frac1k},$$
using $m^{1-a_k}=m^{1/(k-1)}\le n^{1/(k(k-1))}$. Therefore the loop uses at most
$$2k\,n^{1-1/k}+m\ \le\ 2k\,n^{1-1/k}+n^{1/k}$$
colors (the $+m$ counts the colors for the centers $v$).

**Finish.** When the loop ends, the maximum degree is $<f(n,k+1)=n^{1-1/k}$, so Problem 1.5 needs at most $\lceil n^{1-1/k}\rceil$ more colors.

**Total.** $\le(2k+1)\,n^{1-1/k}+n^{1/k}+1\le 2(k+1)\lceil n^{1-1/k}\rceil$ once $n^{1/k}+1\le\lceil n^{1-1/k}\rceil$, which is where the hypothesis $k<\log n$ (and $n$ large compared to $k$) is used (the ceilings absorbing rounding errors). Since $\mathrm{OPT}=k+1$, the ratio is at most $2\lceil n^{1-1/k}\rceil$, completing the induction. $\blacksquare$

*Remark.* The rounding bookkeeping (ceilings and the additive $+1$ per iteration) is only sketched in the official solution; the estimate above is the heart of the argument.

cmimc-2019-power-09.title: Large color classes
cmimc-2019-power-09.body:
We show that at most $3n/\log_kn$ colors are used; since $\mathrm{OPT}=k$ the ratio is $\frac{3n}{k\log_kn}=\frac{3n\log k}{k\log n}$.

**A color class is large.** Let $U$ have $m$ vertices (the induced graph is $k$-colorable). By the pigeonhole principle some color class of an optimal coloring has an independent set of size at least $m/k$; a vertex in such a set has degree at most $m-m/k=m(1-1/k)$ in $G[U]$. So the minimum-degree vertex $v$ chosen by the algorithm has degree $\le m(1-1/k)$, and removing $v$ and its neighbours leaves at least $m/k-1$ vertices in $U$ (about $m/k$). Repeating, the inner loop runs at least $\approx\log_km$ times (until $U$ is empty), and each iteration colors one vertex with $c$; hence one color class has at least $\approx\log_k|W|$ vertices.

**Two phases.**

- *While $|W|>n/\log_kn$:* then $\log_k|W|>\log_kn-\log_k\log_kn>\frac12\log_kn$, so each new color class contains more than $\frac12\log_kn$ vertices. Therefore at most $n\big/\bigl(\tfrac12\log_kn\bigr)=2n/\log_kn$ colors are used in this phase.
- *Once $|W|\le n/\log_kn$:* even giving every remaining vertex its own color costs at most $n/\log_kn$ colors.

In total at most $3n/\log_kn$ colors are used, which gives the claimed approximation ratio. $\blacksquare$

*Remark.* Rounding (the floors in $\log_k$ and the "$-1$" in the number of remaining vertices) is glossed over in the official solution, as here.

cmimc-2019-power-10.title: Fill forced squares
cmimc-2019-power-10.body:
Repeatedly fill any square for which only one number is still possible (it is the only candidate in its row, column or box, or the only number not excluded by its row, column and box). This solves the board without guessing; the unique completion is:

$$\begin{array}{|ccc|ccc|ccc|}\hline
4 & 2 & 6 & 5 & 7 & 1 & 3 & 9 & 8 \\
8 & 5 & 7 & 2 & 9 & 3 & 1 & 4 & 6 \\
1 & 3 & 9 & 4 & 6 & 8 & 2 & 7 & 5 \\ \hline
9 & 7 & 1 & 3 & 8 & 5 & 6 & 2 & 4 \\
5 & 4 & 3 & 7 & 2 & 6 & 8 & 1 & 9 \\
6 & 8 & 2 & 1 & 4 & 9 & 7 & 5 & 3 \\ \hline
7 & 9 & 4 & 6 & 3 & 2 & 5 & 8 & 1 \\
2 & 6 & 5 & 8 & 1 & 4 & 9 & 3 & 7 \\
3 & 1 & 8 & 9 & 5 & 7 & 4 & 6 & 2 \\ \hline
\end{array}$$

(A computer search confirms that this is the only solution.)

cmimc-2019-power-11.title: Pin down the colors
cmimc-2019-power-11.body:
Take a proper $n^2$-coloring of $S'$. The $n^2$ new nodes are mutually adjacent, so they receive $n^2$ distinct colors, i.e. all the colors. Rename the colors (a permutation of the symbols) so that the new node labelled $k$ has color $k$.

Now consider a filled square with value $k$. It is adjacent to the new nodes labelled $j\ne k$, whose colors are all $j\ne k$; so its color cannot be any $j\ne k$, hence it is $k$. Thus every given number keeps its value.

Finally, adjacent squares of the board are adjacent in $S'$, so they have different colors: no row, column or box contains a repeated symbol. The colors of the board squares therefore form a valid completion of the given board (after the renaming of symbols). $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-12.title: Compare with a trivial bound
cmimc-2019-power-12.body:
The optimum is at least $n^2$, since the $n^2$ squares of a single row must carry pairwise different symbols. Any valid filling uses at most one symbol per square, i.e. at most $n^2\cdot n^2=n^4$ distinct symbols. Hence
$$\frac{\text{symbols used}}{\mathrm{OPT}}\le\frac{n^4}{n^2}=n^2.$$
$\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-13.title: Greedy coloring of the Sudoku graph
cmimc-2019-power-13.body:
**Algorithm.** Go through the empty squares in any order. Put in the current square the smallest number in $\{1,2,\dots,3n^2\}$ that does not already appear in its row, in its column or in its box.

**It never gets stuck.** A square shares a unit with the squares of its row ($n^2-1$ others), its column ($n^2-1$ others) and its box ($n^2-1$ others); the row and box overlap in $n-1$ other squares, and the column and box in $n-1$ others. So it has at most $3(n^2-1)-2(n-1)=3n^2-2n-1<3n^2$ neighbours. Hence at most $3n^2-1$ of the $3n^2$ symbols are blocked, and a free symbol always exists (the given squares use symbols $\le n^2\le3n^2$). This is exactly Problem 1.5's greedy bound $\Delta+1\le3n^2$.

**Ratio.** The output is valid and uses at most $3n^2$ symbols while $\mathrm{OPT}\ge n^2$ (indeed $=n^2$ for a completable board), so it is a $3$-approximation. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-14.title: An exact solution of the empty board, then overlay
cmimc-2019-power-14.body:
**Lemma.** The empty board can be filled in polynomial time with $n^2$ symbols. Index rows and columns by $0,\dots,n^2-1$, write a row as $r=qn+s$ with $0\le q,s<n$, and put in square $(r,c)$ the symbol $\bigl(ns+q+c\bigr)\bmod n^2$ (taking residues $0,\dots,n^2-1$). Then:

- *Rows:* in a fixed row the symbol runs over all residues as $c$ varies, so no repetition.
- *Columns:* for fixed $c$ the map $(q,s)\mapsto ns+q$ is a bijection onto $\{0,\dots,n^2-1\}$, so no repetition.
- *Boxes:* a box has fixed $q$ and column $c=Bn+t$ with fixed $B$ and $0\le t<n$ varying; its symbols are $(ns+t)+(q+Bn)\bmod n^2$, and $ns+t$ takes every value in $\{0,\dots,n^2-1\}$ exactly once.

**Algorithm.** Fill the whole board with this pattern using the symbols $n^2+1,\dots,2n^2$ (the pattern shifted up by $n^2$), then overwrite each given square with its given symbol (which lies in $\{1,\dots,n^2\}$).

**Validity.** Two squares sharing a row, column or box: if both are given, they differ because the given board is consistent; if one is given (symbol $\le n^2$) and the other is not (symbol $>n^2$), they differ; if neither is given, they differ by the Lemma.

**Ratio.** At most $2n^2$ symbols are used and $\mathrm{OPT}=n^2$, so this is a $2$-approximation, $k=2<3$. $\blacksquare$

(Better ratios may be possible; the official solution only requires $k<3$ and scores by how small $k$ is.)

cmimc-2019-power-15.title: Send the witness
cmimc-2019-power-15.body:
Let $L\in\mathsf{NP}$ with polynomial-time verifier $A$. On input $w$, the interactive protocol is: $V$ sends $w$ to $P$; $P$ replies with a string $k$; $V$ runs $A(w,k)$ and accepts iff $A$ accepts.

*Completeness.* If $w\in L$ there is a witness $k$ with $A(w,k)$ accepting, and an honest prover sends it, so $V$ accepts.

*Soundness.* If $w\notin L$ then $A(w,k)$ rejects for every $k$, so $V$ rejects whatever $P$ sends: the error probability is $0$ (certainly small).

$V$ runs in polynomial time (reading $k$, whose length may be bounded by the running time of $A$), and uses one round of interaction. Hence $L\in\mathsf{IP}$. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-16a.title: Every edge passes
cmimc-2019-power-16a.body: If $G$ is $3$-colorable, $P$ uses a proper $3$-coloring, permuted by a random permutation of the colors; permuting colors preserves properness. So for every edge $(u,v)$ that $V$ may ask for, the revealed colors satisfy $a\ne b$, and $V$ accepts in every round. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-16b.title: A bad edge exists
cmimc-2019-power-16b.body:
Suppose $G$ is not $3$-colorable. Whatever assignment of the colors $1,2,3$ to the vertices $P$ commits to (it is fixed before $V$ chooses the edge), it is not a proper coloring, so at least one edge $e$ has both endpoints of the same color.

$V$ chooses the edge uniformly at random, so asks for such an edge with probability at least $1/|E|$, in which case $a=b$ and $V$ rejects. Thus in one iteration the probability that $P$ is not caught is at most $1-\frac1{|E|}$. Over $r$ independent iterations the error probability is at most $\left(1-\frac1{|E|}\right)^r\le e^{-r/|E|}$, which is exponentially small for $r\gg|E|$. $\blacksquare$

cmimc-2019-power-16c.title: Simulate the transcript
cmimc-2019-power-16c.body:
In one round, $V$ sees an edge $(u,v)$ (chosen by $V$) and the revealed colors $(a,b)$ with $a\ne b$ (a proper coloring has distinct colors on an edge). The coloring committed in that round is $\pi\circ\chi$ for a fixed proper coloring $\chi$ and a uniformly random permutation $\pi$ of $\{1,2,3\}$. For $\chi(u)\ne\chi(v)$, the pair $(\pi(\chi(u)),\pi(\chi(v)))$ is uniformly distributed over the $6$ ordered pairs of distinct colors, whatever $\chi$ is.

The *simulator* receives the edge $V$ asks for and outputs $(a,b)$ uniformly at random among the $6$ ordered pairs of distinct colors. Its output has exactly the same distribution as the real transcript, so $V$ learns nothing from the protocol beyond the fact that the edge is properly colored (nothing about the coloring $\chi$ itself). Since the colors are re-randomized in each repetition, the same holds for the whole sequence of rounds. $\blacksquare$
